summary: A sound translation with a few real faults. 24:19 has the wrong tense ("had finished" in her promise) and two false grammar notes; 24:22 adds "nose-ring" where the verse has only נֶזֶם, and the note and Ibn Ezra's summary wrongly make him say this one is a nose-ring; Radak's summary at 24:19 was wrong. Style and context patches: 24:24 relative clause, the camels dispute (24:19), Nahor's family (24:24), the missing rulings. Ibn Ezra's hifil reading of לָלִין is correctly recorded, not adopted.

patches.value: And she finished giving him drink, and said, "I will draw for your camels too, until they have finished drinking."
patches.reason: In her promise the clause is future: until they have finished, not "had finished".

value.english: And she finished giving him drink
I will draw for your camels too
value.literal: 'also to-camels-your I-will-draw': the Hebrew puts גַּם first

patches.reason: The English changed; the last phrase follows it.
Tense follows the English.

patches.value: גַּם stands before its noun as in Hebrew (גַּם לִגְמַלֶּיךָ); the English puts "too" after "your camels".
patches.reason: The note said "after the verb"; the English has "too" after "your camels".

value: The etnaḥta on לְהַשְׁקֹתוֹ closes the first clause; the revia on וַתֹּאמֶר is a disjunctive, and the speech follows it.
גַּם comes before its object, as in Hebrew, 'also for your camels'; the English puts 'too' after 'your camels'.
עַד אִם כִּלּוּ לִשְׁתֹּת: the temporal clause 'until' with אִם; the piel perfect כִּלּוּ has the camels as subject.
The piel כִּלּוּ is used without an object, 'they have finished' (drinking), and the infinitive לִשְׁתֹּת names the act.
patches.reason: Two notes were untrue: the placing of "too", and the tense.

patches.value: Radak: 'but if they finish drinking, then I will stop' (I will draw for them until they finish drinking); or אִם stands in place of אֲשֶׁר, 'until they finish drinking'. The English takes the first.
patches.reason: The summary said "until they are able to drink"; Radak writes עַד אֲשֶׁר יְכַלּוּ לִשְׁתּוֹת, "until they finish drinking".

value: Camels drink large quantities of water after a long journey; the verse's own detail (until they had finished drinking) shows why the drawing took long.

Whether domesticated camels were in use as pack and riding animals in the patriarchal period is disputed: some hold that they came into common use only late in the second millennium BCE, others find earlier evidence. The English says 'camels' and takes no side.
patches.reason: Decisions: where the evidence on camels is in dispute, the context notes name the positions.

patches.value: Radak: this shows she was well brought up: she did not know who he was and still called him 'my lord', and she hurried to give him water, and gave it from her hand.
patches.reason: The summary left out Radak's point (בַּת מוּסָר, "of good upbringing") and his "from her hand".
אִם in הֲ ... אִם־לֹא is the disjunctive "or" of a double question, BDB 2 (interrogative particle), not "if".

patches.value: And it came to pass, when the camels had finished drinking, that the man took a gold ring of half a shekel by weight, and two bracelets on her hands, ten shekels of gold by weight.
patches.reason: נֶזֶם alone: the verse does not say it is a nose-ring (24:47 says he put it on her nose; Ibn Ezra says a נֶזֶם may be for nose or ear). The English adds what this verse lacks.

patches.value: נֶזֶם: a ring; Ibn Ezra says it may be worn in the nose or in the ear, and 24:47 has the servant put it on her nose. The entry gives no senses.
patches.reason: The note said Ibn Ezra makes this a nose-ring; he gives both uses.

patches.value: gold as measure of weight; the Hebrew names no unit, and 'shekels' is added in the English, understood from בֶּקַע 'half (a shekel)' and the Targum's סִלְעִין
patches.reason: The note called "shekels" the text's own measure; the text does not name it.
Of things worn (bracelets): BDB II.1.a.(a).

patches.value: The Hebrew names no unit for the ten; the English supplies 'shekels', understood from בֶּקַע, half a shekel (Ibn Ezra), and the Targum's סִלְעִין. The ring is given as a ring, as the verse says; 24:47 places it on her nose. The ring and bracelets are given by weight, not by piece.
patches.reason: The note called the shekel the text's unit; it is understood, not stated.

patches.value: Ibn Ezra: there is a נֶזֶם worn in the nose and also in the ear; the one on the nose hangs down from a cord tied on the forehead.
patches.reason: The summary said "this one is the nose-ring"; Ibn Ezra speaks of the word in general.

value: The shekel was a unit of weight; gold and silver were weighed in shekels before coined money came into use in the region. The text gives the weight of the gold, not the number of pieces.

This verse does not say where the ring went; at 24:47 the servant says he put it on her nose. Ibn Ezra says a נֶזֶם may be worn in the nose or in the ear, and that the nose kind hangs from a cord tied on the forehead.
patches.reason: The note said the text puts this one on the nose; this verse does not.

patches.value: And she said to him, "I am the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor."
patches.reason: "who bore to Nahor" reads as if Milcah bore to Nahor with no object and attaches to Milcah only; אֲשֶׁר is the relative of Bethuel, "whom she bore". The accent (zaqef gadol on Milcah) separates the clause.

value: Nahor was Abraham's brother, and Milcah, his wife, was the daughter of their brother Haran (11:27–29; 22:20–23); Bethuel was thus Abraham's nephew and Rebekah his great-niece.
patches.reason: A reader needs the relationship the verse assumes.

value.summary: Ramban: cites Rashi (he ran because he saw the water rise) and Bereshit Rabbah on 'she filled her jar and went up'; he thinks the rabbis drew the miracle from that wording and that it happened the first time, and that the servant did not tell it to the family (24:45) lest they not believe.

verdicts.comment: 'Astonished at her' carries his 'for her sake' (about her); the hitpaʿel is kept and the root שָׁתָה is not used.
After the patch the English says only 'ring', which fits his both uses.
'Two bracelets', one on each hand, follows him.
He reads a hifil; the pack's data is a qal infinitive. The data is kept and his reading recorded (token note, ruling, apparatus); 'for us to lodge' fits either reading.
